gaps.construct: Return (x, err): a partial value alongside the error
gaps.description: Scribe failures carry no value and a failed operation produces nothing, so the partially decoded x returned with an error is lost.

gaps.construct: Pass through any error from r.ReadByte unchanged
gaps.description: `fails with` requires a closed list of failure names; an arbitrary error from an interface implementation has no name. Invented catch-all ReadError.
No interfaces; treated as a capability type, which hides that any implementation can be passed.
No bitwise and/or/shift and no hex literals; invented `bitand`, `bitor`, `shifted left by`, and wrote 128/127 in decimal.

gaps.construct: uint64, byte, and explicit conversion uint64(b)
gaps.description: No fixed-width types and no explicit conversion form even though implicit conversion is banned. Invented `UInt64`, `Byte`, `b as a UInt64`.

gaps.construct: if i > 0 && err == io.EOF { err = io.ErrUnexpectedEOF }
gaps.description: Inspecting and rewriting an error needs a nested handle block with one on failure line per name, including a line that just re-fails with the same name.

gaps.construct: Typed zero-initialised locals (var x uint64; var s uint)
gaps.description: `var` has no type annotation, and the literal 0 does not fix the type.

notes: The control flow (bounded loop, early return, explicit errors) maps well, and `fails with EOF, UnexpectedEOF, ReadError, Overflow` is clearer than Go's `error`. The losses are all at the edges: partial results on failure, open error sets from interfaces, and the byte-level numeric vocabulary that every binary decoder needs.
